---
title: "Terminology Traps"
---

Several words in this field are used in more than one sense, and several methods are called by names
that suggest more (or less) than they are. Each trap below is stated, then corrected, with the chapter
where the correction is derived.

**"RLHF" names a pipeline, not an algorithm.** Supervised fine-tuning, a reward model fit to human
comparisons, then RL against it (usually PPO) with a KL penalty to the SFT model. Replace any stage and
it is still called RLHF. ([The Shared Target, and RLHF with PPO](chapters/06-the-shared-target.qmd))

**"PPO" in LLM papers is not quite the PPO of the original paper.** Original PPO already had a
KL-penalty *variant*, but its KL was to $\pi_{\text{old}}$, the policy that generated the batch: a soft
trust region. LLM "PPO" adds a KL to a *fixed* reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, usually folded into the
per-token reward, which changes the objective and gives it the closed-form optimum $\pi^\star$.
([Keeping Updates Stable](chapters/03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd))

**DPO is not RL in the sense of sampling and rewarding, but it targets an RL optimum.** It never samples
from the policy and never evaluates a reward during training; with infinite data its minimizer is
exactly the KL-regularized optimum that RLHF aims at. Which sense matters depends on the question.
([Direct Preference Methods](chapters/07-direct-preference-methods.qmd))

**"On-policy" usually means "approximately on-policy".** PPO, GRPO and their variants reuse each batch
for several updates, and asynchronous systems train on samples a few versions old. Importance ratios and
clipping are what make that workable. ([Keeping Updates Stable](chapters/03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd),
[What RL Actually Does to a Model](chapters/11-what-rl-does-to-a-model.qmd))

**"Offline" and "off-policy" are different.** Off-policy methods learn from samples of a different
policy, usually correcting with importance weights. Offline methods learn from a fixed dataset and never
collect more. DPO is offline; PPO is slightly off-policy; online DPO is neither.
([Direct Preference Methods](chapters/07-direct-preference-methods.qmd))

**"Reward model", "verifier", "judge" and "critic" are four different things.** A reward model is a
network trained to output a score; a verifier is a rule or program that checks correctness; a judge is a
general model prompted to compare or grade; a critic is a value function trained during RL to predict
future reward from a partial response, used as a baseline. The first three produce rewards; the fourth
estimates their expectation. ([Where Rewards Come From](chapters/05-rewards.qmd))

**Reward, return, value and advantage are four different quantities.** A reward scores one step or one
response; the return sums future rewards; a value is the *expected* return from a state; an advantage is
how much better an action is than the policy's average in that state.
([What Makes a Problem RL](chapters/01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd))

**"KL penalty" does not say which KL, or how it is implemented.** Forward and reverse KL ask for different
things (mass-covering vs mode-seeking), and a KL estimator's implementation decides which one is actually
regularized: "$k_1$ in the reward" follows the reverse KL, "$k_3$ as a loss" follows the forward KL.
([Keeping Updates Stable](chapters/03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd))

**"Unbiased" is about a specific quantity.** The $k_3$ estimator is an unbiased estimate of the KL's
*value* under on-policy samples; its gradient as a loss is not the gradient of that KL. A leave-one-out
baseline leaves the policy gradient unbiased; the group mean including the sample itself shrinks it.
([Keeping Updates Stable](chapters/03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd), [Policy Gradients](chapters/02-policy-gradients.qmd))

**"Group normalization" is not just variance reduction.** Dividing each prompt's advantages by their
standard deviation reweights prompts by difficulty and weakens the KL relative to the reward; it changes
the objective. ([Policy Gradients Without a Critic](chapters/08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd))

**"Calibrated" is a property of a model on a distribution.** A model can be calibrated when results are
pooled and miscalibrated within every slice, as the independent evaluation of Jev found.
([Rewarding Calibration](chapters/10-rewarding-calibration.qmd))

**"RLCD" names two unrelated methods.** Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation (2023)
builds preference pairs from contrasting prompts; Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (2026)
is TypeSafe AI's undisclosed training method for calibrated probabilities.
([Rewarding Calibration](chapters/10-rewarding-calibration.qmd))
